Priya Nandakumar, a chartered structural engineer at Torrent Structures, discovers while reusing an old spreadsheet that a load factor was entered incorrectly in the design of steel balconies on a recently occupied residential block. Her quick check suggests the balcony connections have a much smaller safety margin than intended, though failure is not certain. Her manager, worried about liability and the client relationship, tells her to 'leave it until the next maintenance inspection in two years'.

Analyse Priya's ethical and legal position and set out the steps she should take.
markScheme: Identifies principle of holding public safety paramount (responsibility to society in the 2026 Statement; respect for life, law, the environment and public good in the 2017 version)
Honesty and integrity: cannot conceal known error
Accuracy and rigour: verify the calculation promptly and independently
Leadership and communication: raise concern clearly and in writing
Legal duties: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974; duties to those affected by work; Building Safety Act 2022 context for residential buildings
Professional code of conduct of her institution and Engineering Council obligations
Steps: verify, document, escalate internally above manager, consider interim measures (restrict balcony use, temporary props)
Informing client and building owner/regulator if internal route fails
Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 protection for whistleblowing; confidential reporting routes (e.g. CROSS)
Weighs consequences for employer but concludes safety overrides; reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Priya faces a conflict between loyalty to her employer and her duty to the public. The Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering Statement of Ethical Principles (updated 2026) includes responsibility to society, which covers reporting unsafe practice, and professional institution codes require members to put public safety first and to raise concerns about danger. Waiting two years with a known, unquantified risk to occupants would breach that duty.

Honesty and integrity rule out concealing an error once found, even one made by the firm itself. Accuracy and rigour require her first to confirm the problem: rechecking the calculation, ideally with an independent colleague, quantifying the actual margin and identifying which connections are affected. Leadership and communication require her to report clearly, in writing, rather than letting the matter drop.

Legally, the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 places duties on employers and employees not to expose others to risk from their work, and designers carry duties under the CDM Regulations 2015. If the block is a higher-risk building (in England, at least 18 m or seven storeys with at least two residential units), the Building Safety Act 2022 regime adds further duties. The firm's liability exposure would be far worse if a balcony failed after the error was known and ignored.

Steps: (1) verify and document the error and its consequences promptly; (2) present the findings in writing to her manager, explaining the risk; (3) if the manager still refuses, escalate within the firm to a director or the person responsible for technical quality; (4) recommend immediate interim measures, such as restricting balcony use or installing temporary supports, while a permanent fix is designed; (5) ensure the client and building owner are informed, since they control the building; (6) if the firm will not act, report to the relevant authority. The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 protects workers making qualifying disclosures about health and safety dangers, and confidential safety reporting schemes exist for structural concerns. Her institution can also advise.

The short-term cost to the client relationship is real, but public safety overrides it, and prompt, transparent correction is also the firm's best protection.

questions.q:
Linnet Lighting is redesigning an outdoor LED floodlight. Data per unit: aluminium body 2.0 kg (primary aluminium 200 MJ/kg; recycled 30 MJ/kg); polycarbonate lens 0.3 kg (110 MJ/kg); electronics 150 MJ (total); manufacture 40 MJ; transport 10 MJ. Use: 50 W for 4000 h per year over 10 years; electricity generated at 40% efficiency (primary energy basis).

(a) Perform an eco-audit of primary energy by life phase and identify the dominant phase. (b) Evaluate two proposals: switching to recycled aluminium, or a driver and optics upgrade that cuts power by 10%. (c) Using your results, critically discuss the claim that "sustainable engineering is mainly about choosing green materials", considering circular-economy and ethical dimensions.
markScheme: Manufacture 40 MJ, transport 10 MJ
Use: 50 W × 40 000 h = 2000 kWh = 7200 MJ electrical; primary 7200/0.4 = 18 000 MJ
Total ≈ 18 600 MJ; use ≈ 97%
Recycled Al saves 2.0 × 170 = 340 MJ ≈ 1.8%
10% power cut saves 1800 MJ ≈ 9.7%, about five times more
Use phase dominates, so efficiency first; materials matter for passive products
Circular economy: durability, repairability (replaceable driver), modular design, end-of-life recovery of aluminium
Limitations: single metric (energy), grid decarbonisation lowers use-phase share over time, data uncertainty, LCA to ISO 14040/14044 for robust decisions
Ethical dimension: public good and environment in professional codes, avoiding greenwashing, net zero 2050 target
Balanced conclusion: material choice matters but must be targeted by life-phase analysis
Accurate calculation and clear structure
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Material energy: aluminium 2.0 × 200 = 400 MJ; polycarbonate 0.3 × 110 = 33 MJ; electronics 150 MJ; total 583 MJ. Manufacture 40 MJ and transport 10 MJ. Use: 50 W × 4000 h × 10 years = 2000 kWh = 7200 MJ of electricity, equivalent to 7200/0.40 = 18 000 MJ of primary energy. The total is about 18 600 MJ, so use accounts for roughly 97% and materials about 3%.

(b) Recycled aluminium saves 2.0 × (200 − 30) = 340 MJ, about 1.8% of the total. A 10% power reduction saves 0.10 × 18 000 = 1800 MJ, about 9.7%, more than five times as much. The driver and optics upgrade should be prioritised, though both can be adopted if cost allows, since recycled aluminium also cuts mining impacts not captured by an energy metric.

(c) The claim is misleading for energy-using products. For this floodlight, material choice affects only a few per cent of life-cycle energy, while efficient electronics, optics that place light only where needed, and controls such as dimming and presence sensing dominate. For passive products, such as furniture, packaging or structures, materials and manufacture do dominate, so the right strategy depends on life-phase analysis rather than a general rule.

Sustainability also goes beyond embodied energy. Circular-economy principles favour long life, repairability (a replaceable driver often outlasts a sealed unit), modular upgrades and easy separation of aluminium for high-value recycling at end of life. Electricity grids are decarbonising, so the use-phase share will shrink over time, gradually raising the relative importance of materials. A full LCA to ISO 14040/14044 would test these conclusions across impacts such as CO₂, toxicity and resource depletion.

Ethically, professional codes require engineers to respect the environment and public good, and the UK's statutory net zero 2050 target sets the direction. Claiming sustainability by switching to green materials while ignoring the dominant use phase risks greenwashing. Engineers should base decisions on honest, quantified analysis and target the life phase where the impact actually lies.
